content:
Let  

\[
S_r=\sum_{\substack{0\le k\le 10000\\k\equiv r\pmod{502}}}\binom{10000}{k},
\qquad r=0,1,\dots ,501 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Roots‑of‑unity filter in \(\mathbf F_{503}\)

Because \(503\) is prime, \(\mathbf F_{503}^{\times}\) is cyclic of order  

\[
502=503-1 .
\]

Let \(g\) be a generator of \(\mathbf F_{503}^{\times}\); then \(g^{0},g^{1},\dots ,g^{501}\) are all the non‑zero residues modulo \(503\).
For any integer \(N\),

\[
\sum_{k\equiv r\;(502)}\binom{N}{k}
 =\frac1{502}\sum_{j=0}^{501} g^{-jr}(1+g^{j})^{N}
\tag{1}
\]

(the usual discrete Fourier filter, now taken in the field \(\mathbf F_{503}\)).

Taking \(N=10000\) and using (1),

\[
S_r\equiv 502^{-1}\sum_{j=0}^{501} g^{-jr}(1+g^{j})^{10000}\pmod{503}.
\]

Since \(502\equiv-1\pmod{503}\), its inverse is also \(-1\); hence  

\[
S_r\equiv -\sum_{j=0}^{501} g^{-jr}(1+g^{j})^{10000}\pmod{503}.
\tag{2}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Reducing the exponent

For any \(a\neq0\pmod{503}\), Fermat’s little theorem gives \(a^{502}\equiv1\pmod{503}\).
Write  

\[
10000 = 502\cdot19 + 462 .
\]

Thus for each \(j\) with \(1+g^{j}\not\equiv0\),

\[
(1+g^{j})^{10000}\equiv (1+g^{j})^{462}\pmod{503}.
\]

If \(1+g^{j}\equiv0\) (this happens for exactly one \(j\)), the term is \(0\).
Hence (2) becomes

\[
S_r\equiv -\sum_{j=0}^{501} g^{-jr}(1+g^{j})^{462}\pmod{503}.
\tag{3}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Binomial expansion

\[
(1+g^{j})^{462}= \sum_{k=0}^{462}\binom{462}{k}g^{jk}.
\]

Insert this into (3) and interchange the sums:

\[
S_r\equiv -\sum_{k=0}^{462}\binom{462}{k}
        \Bigl(\sum_{j=0}^{501} g^{j(k-r)}\Bigr)\pmod{503}.
\]

The inner sum is a geometric series.  
If \(k\equiv r\pmod{502}\) it equals \(502\); otherwise it is \(0\).
Since \(0\le k\le462<502\), the condition \(k\equiv r\pmod{502}\) is simply \(k=r\).

Therefore  

\[
S_r\equiv
\begin{cases}
-\binom{462}{r}\,502 &\text{if }0\le r\le 462,\\[4pt]
0 &\text{if }463\le r\le 501 .
\end{cases}
\]

Now \(502\equiv-1\pmod{503}\), so \(-\!502\equiv1\pmod{503}\). Consequently  

\[
S_r\equiv
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\binom{462}{r}\pmod{503} & (0\le r\le462),\\[6pt]
0\pmod{503} & (463\le r\le501).
\end{cases}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  When is \(S_r\) a multiple of \(503\)?

The prime \(503\) exceeds \(462\). Hence none of the binomial coefficients
\(\binom{462}{r}\;(0\le r\le462)\) is divisible by \(503\) (the numerator and
denominator contain no factor \(503\)). Thus

\[
S_r\not\equiv0\pmod{503}\quad\text{for }0\le r\le462,
\]
while  

\[
S_r\equiv0\pmod{503}\quad\text{for }463\le r\le501 .
\]

The values of \(r\) for which \(S_r\) is a multiple of \(503\) are  

\[
r=463,464,\dots ,501.
\]

The count of such integers is  

\[
501-463+1 = 39 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
\[
\boxed{39}
\]
